query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases? Earlier studies of refractory and transition-metal-based high-entropy alloys primarily examined elemental and compositional effects involving Al, Cr, Si, Ti, and V, but the reported outcomes depended on composition limits, phase readjustment, and processing. This emphasis has not resolved the oxidation behavior of compositionally complex alloys, for which synergistic elemental effects make interpretation difficult. The starting alloy was designed to retain an fcc matrix for formability and has demonstrated notable strength and fatigue performance, so any explanation should account for its integrity without compromising those constraints. Define a controlled comparison that would distinguish the proposed explanation, predict observations relative to the starting-state baseline, identify applicable exposure boundaries and supporting prior evidence, and state an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Oxidation-induced degradation of the additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy is governed by the formation and local destabilization of a protective (Al,Cr)-rich oxide scale, whose integrity depends on partial pressure of reactive gases. Under moderate oxidative conditions, a continuous scale forms and protects the fcc matrix, but in more aggressive oxidizing or reducing atmospheres, local depletion of Al and Cr near boundaries disrupts scale continuity, accelerates inward diffusion of oxygen, and promotes secondary phase evolution, thereby reducing mechanical integrity.
generation.material_initial_state: Additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, in the as-solidified (post-process) condition, retaining its formability and high strength/fatigue performance.
generation.intervention: Control of gas atmosphere composition and partial pressures during 600–900 °C exposure to either oxidizing (O2-rich) or reducing (H2-rich) environments, combined with real-time in-situ observations and thermodynamic modeling.
generation.conditions: Samples held at 600–900 °C in adjustable partial pressures of O2 and H2 for up to 100 h, representative of high-temperature service conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Local partitioning of Al and Cr into forming oxide layers at free surfaces and grain boundaries, including the possible formation of secondary B2- or Laves-type phases consuming Al/Cr and reducing the protective oxide’s continuity.
generation.mechanism: Under moderately oxidizing partial pressures, Al and Cr segregate to surfaces and form a stable protective oxide. However, in aggressive conditions (either high pO2 or strongly reducing atmospheres), these oxide layers are disrupted or spall, causing accelerated oxygen ingress, internal oxidation, and microstructural damage near grain boundaries.
generation.predicted_outcome: When partial pressures of oxygen are set within an intermediate range, a continuous (Al,Cr)-rich oxide scale will persist, maintaining near-baseline mechanical strength. More extreme or reducing atmospheres will degrade scale integrity, leading to oxygen ingress, internal oxidation products, and reduced mechanical performance relative to the baseline.
generation.baseline: As-produced alloy specimens tested in inert or mild gas atmospheres, which maintain a largely intact oxide scale and exhibit stable strength/fatigue behavior.
generation.boundary: For temperatures below ~600 °C or short exposures, limited oxidation occurs and scale disruption is minimal. Above ~900 °C, or very high pO2, or with strongly reducing conditions, the protective scale is more likely to spall or degrade. The capacity for Al and Cr to re-form a protective oxide during repeated thermal cycling and under complex gas chemistries remains uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: It is unclear whether kinetically sluggish diffusion of Al and Cr in the fcc matrix alone can achieve or maintain a uniform oxide layer under these varied gas atmospheres. Further, the exact partial pressure at which scale disruption initiates is not well established.

falsification_experiment.design: Subject replicate specimens to in-situ high-temperature environmental microscopy while systematically varying partial pressures of O2 and H2. Track real-time scale evolution and measure oxygen uptake rates via thermogravimetry.
measurements: Cross-sectional oxide thickness and composition by electron microscopy (SEM/EDS).
In-situ scale integrity and thickness over time by environmental TEM.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If stable protective oxide layers form and remain intact, preventing significant oxygen ingress and preserving mechanical performance even under more extreme oxidizing or reducing conditions, this would contradict the proposed reliance on partial-pressure-sensitive oxide layer destabilization for high-temperature degradation.

cited_evidence.text: Structural metallic materials for applications at high temperatures must have a balance of mechanical properties and oxidation resistance. Coated and internally cooled Ni-based superalloys are used in gas turbine engines close to their high temperature limit, which is imposed by the melting temperature of Ni. The search for new alloys with similar or better capabilities at higher temperatures has concentrated on Nb-silicide based alloys that have lower densities, significantly higher solidus temperatures in excess of 1900 °C and can offer notable mechanical properties []. For example, some of these alloys can have compressive yield strength of about 1800 MPa at room temperature, 1200 MPa at 1000 °C and 500 MPa at 1200 °C []. cited_evidence.text: Zone A formation was observed in the alloy MG7 and layered microstructures formed in the alloys MG7 and OHC5 [,]. Common in all these alloys was the simultaneous presence of Al, Si, and Ti and solute macrosegregation. Note that in the alloy OHC3, which did not contain Si and Ti, a Zone A did not form even though the alloy was Al-rich. Considering the maps in the Figure 8, if Zone A formation in the BC alloy were to be required, the alloy should have δ > 6, VEC > 3.75 and Δχ > 0.1. BC alloys with Al, Cr, Hf, Nb, Si, and Ti-alloying elements compatible with metallic UHTM substrates with Nb and Si addition could be designed/selected to have the parameters δ, VEC, and Δχ in the as-manufactured condition and after exposure to high temperature, respectively, in the ranges 6 < δ < 10.5, 3.75 < VEC < 4.5 and 0.1 < Δχ < 0.16.
